title: Two Eagles, a Vine, and a Tender Sprig
summary: Ezekiel tells a riddle about a great eagle that plucks the top of a cedar and plants a low vine, and a second eagle toward which the vine turns its roots. God explains: the king of Babylon took Judah's king to Babylon and set up a new king under oath, but that king broke the covenant by turning to Egypt, and he will die in Babylon. The chapter ends with God himself planting a tender sprig from the cedar on a high mountain of Israel, where it will grow into a majestic cedar sheltering birds of every kind.
story: Chapter 17 is the last of three pictures of Jerusalem in chapters 15 to 17, following the useless vine and the unfaithful wife. Where chapter 16 surveyed the city's whole history, chapter 17 zooms in on current events: the reign of Zedekiah and his fatal decision to rebel against Babylon. It also carries forward chapter 12's prediction that the prince would be taken to Babylon and die there. Most importantly, it ends with the book's first clear promise about the royal line of David. After the judgment on the last kings of Judah, God will plant a new shoot from the same cedar, a promise that Ezekiel develops in chapters 34 and 37, where he speaks of a coming shepherd-king from David's line.
historical:
The riddle maps onto recent history, and verses 12 to 21 spell it out. The first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar II, king of Babylon. The top of the cedar is King Jehoiachin, whom Nebuchadnezzar took to Babylon in 597 BC along with his officials (2 Kings 24:10-16); Babylon is the land of merchants. The seed of the land is Zedekiah, Jehoiachin's uncle, whom Nebuchadnezzar made king and bound by a covenant oath (2 Kings 24:17). 2 Chronicles 36:13 adds that Nebuchadnezzar had made him swear by God, which explains why God calls the broken oath “My oath” (verse 19). For a time Judah survived as a low, spreading vine: a humbled but living vassal kingdom.

The second eagle is the pharaoh of Egypt. Zedekiah sent envoys to Egypt seeking horses and troops (verse 15) and rebelled against Babylon. The pharaoh at the time was either Psammetichus II or his successor Apries, called Hophra in Jeremiah 44:30; the exact timing of Zedekiah's approach is debated. Jeremiah 37:5-11 records that an Egyptian army did march out and briefly forced the Babylonians to lift the siege of Jerusalem, but it withdrew, and the siege resumed. One of the Lachish letters, military messages written on pottery shortly before the fall, mentions a commander of Judah's army going down to Egypt, which many scholars connect with this appeal. Jerusalem fell in 587 or 586 BC, and Zedekiah was blinded and taken to Babylon, where he died (2 Kings 25:6-7).
cultural:
Treaties in the ancient Near East were solemn oaths sworn in the names of the gods, and breaking one was treated as a crime against those gods as well as against the overlord. Surviving Assyrian vassal treaties list terrible curses on any vassal who rebels. Ezekiel assumes this world: Zedekiah had given his hand in pledge (verse 18), a gesture of sworn commitment. What is striking is that God treats the oath to a pagan king as binding, because it was sworn in his name. Breaking it was treason against the LORD himself (verse 20).

The images were familiar too. The eagle (or possibly the griffon vulture, since the Hebrew word covers both) was a symbol of power and speed. The cedar of Lebanon was the grandest tree in the region and was used in royal palaces and in Solomon's temple, so the top of the cedar fits the royal house of David. A spreading vine low to the ground and a tree sheltering birds were well-known pictures of a kingdom, the second especially of a great empire that gives protection to many peoples (compare Daniel 4:10-12).
literary: God calls the chapter a riddle and a parable (verse 2), and it unfolds in three parts. The riddle itself (verses 1 to 10) is a fable with birds and plants, ending with pointed questions: “Will it flourish?” The interpretation (verses 11 to 21) translates it into political history and then into theology: Zedekiah's broken oath is also a broken covenant with God. The final oracle (verses 22 to 24) returns to the image of the cedar, but now God himself is the planter, not a foreign king. The chapter moves from what the eagles did to what God will do, and its last verse gathers the whole book's theme of reversal into a single line: “I bring the tall tree down and make the low tree tall.”

outline.t: The riddle: the first eagle, the cedar top, and the low vine
The second eagle, and the vine that turns toward it
The meaning: Babylon, Zedekiah, and the broken oath
God plants a tender sprig on the mountain of Israel

doctrines.note: Kings and empires appear as eagles moving plants from place to place, but the chapter ends with God doing the planting. He brings the tall tree down and makes the low tree tall (verse 24). The rise and fall of nations is under his rule.

Zedekiah's covenant with Babylon was sworn in God's name, so breaking it was breaking faith with God (verse 19). The chapter shows that God holds his people to their word, even when it is given to a pagan ruler.

The tender sprig from the top of the cedar (verse 22) points to a future king from David's line whom God himself will raise up. This fits the wider prophetic hope of a righteous branch from David (Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5), which the New Testament finds fulfilled in Jesus.

words.note: Chidah, riddle. It refers to an enigmatic saying whose meaning must be worked out, like Samson's riddle in Judges 14 or the hard questions the queen of Sheba brought to Solomon. Ezekiel's fable is a riddle because its political meaning is hidden in images, inviting hearers to think before the answer is given.

Erez, cedar. The cedars of Lebanon were famous for their size and fine wood, and they were the prized material for royal and sacred buildings. In this chapter the cedar represents the royal house of David, and its topmost shoots its kings.

Alah, oath. It refers to a sworn commitment, often with a curse attached to anyone who breaks it. Zedekiah despised the oath (verses 16, 18, 19), and God calls it his own. The same word appears in 16:59, where Jerusalem despised the oath by breaking the covenant with God.

Yoneqet, shoot or young twig, from a root connected with suckling, and so describing something young and tender. In verse 22 God plucks a tender shoot from the top of the cedar. The image of a young shoot from a royal tree became a standard picture of the coming king.

christ: The closing promise (verses 22 to 24) belongs to the prophetic hope of a new king from David's line, which Isaiah pictures as a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isaiah 11:1) and Jeremiah as a righteous branch (Jeremiah 23:5). The New Testament presents Jesus as the son of David who fulfills that hope. Jesus also described the kingdom of God as a mustard seed that grows into a plant large enough for birds to nest in its branches (Mark 4:30-32), an image close to this chapter's cedar sheltering birds of every kind, and many interpreters hear Ezekiel in it. The reversal of verse 24, the tall brought low and the low made tall, echoes through Mary's song (Luke 1:52), where God brings down rulers and lifts up the humble. The links are real echoes; Ezekiel does not name Jesus, but he points to the kind of king and kingdom the gospel announces.

hard.q: Why does God hold Zedekiah to an oath sworn to a pagan conqueror who had invaded Judah?
hard.a: It can seem strange for God to side with Babylon's claims over his own people. Ezekiel's reasoning is twofold. First, the oath was sworn in the LORD's name (2 Chronicles 36:13), and Israel's law treated such oaths as sacred (Numbers 30:2); to swear by God and then break the oath was to treat his name as worthless. Second, the prophets of this period, Jeremiah as well as Ezekiel, taught that submission to Babylon was God's judgment on Judah for its sin, and that rebellion against it was rebellion against God's discipline (Jeremiah 27). Some readers worry that this makes God an ally of empire. The chapter answers that worry in its final verses, where God, not Babylon, plants the true king, and brings the tall tree down. Babylon's power is permitted for a time, not endorsed forever.

questions: Zedekiah sought security from Egypt rather than keeping his word. Where are you tempted to break a commitment because another option looks safer?
The chapter takes an oath sworn to a pagan king seriously because it was sworn in God's name. How seriously do you take your promises?
God says he brings the tall tree down and makes the low tree tall. Where have you seen that reversal in your own life or in history?
